conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers make sense of the emotional ups and downs that can come after a baby arrives. Today I’d like to do a quick check-in with you using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually shortened to the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screening that looks at how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. It can flag anything from mild “baby blues” to more significant anxiety or depressive symptoms, and it even has a question about self-harm so we can be sure you’re safe.

Your answers stay between you and the care team, and there’s no right or wrong response—only what’s true for you. We’ll take one question at a time, and if any question feels hard to talk about, just let me know and we can slow down. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.

Here’s the first question:  
In the past week, have you found yourself still able to look forward to things, or has that sense of enjoyment been hard to come by?

Honestly… I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my sister texts that she’s stopping by with coffee—but they fade fast. I’ll think, “Great, a visitor,” and then feel too tired or distracted to enjoy it once she’s here. Things that used to feel fun—watching a show with my husband, even taking a walk—now feel more like chores I “should” do. So I guess I do look forward to stuff, just not as much, and when it happens it feels kind of flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh—maybe once a day—like when the baby let out this tiny burp that sounded like grandpa. But it’s short-lived; the giggle feels kind of thin, and then I’m right back to tired. So yes, I find funny moments, just not as hearty or as often as before.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to plan little things—like ordering my favorite take-out on Friday—but when the food actually arrives I’m just picking at it. I still make myself look forward, otherwise the days feel endless, but the happy “buzz” I used to get isn’t really there. So I guess I look forward, yet the enjoyment part feels kind of muted.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week. Yesterday the baby was fussy for almost an hour and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or I wasn’t burping her right. My husband finally calmed her in two minutes and I felt like I’d failed. I know, rationally, babies just cry, but the “what did I do wrong?” voice pops up more than it should.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little. Like, I’ll be feeding her and suddenly wonder if the formula is too warm or if she’s breathing okay even though she’s right there, perfectly fine. It’s not all day—just quick flashes a few times—but they come out of nowhere and my heart races for a minute before I talk myself down.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—more like a sudden “what-if” rush. One night I heard a car door outside and my mind jumped to someone breaking in, even though we live in a safe neighborhood. My stomach tightened for maybe thirty seconds, then it passed. Nothing full-blown, just those quick surges that leave me feeling silly afterward.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Like yesterday—she wouldn’t nap, laundry was piled, and I needed to pump. I felt this pressure in my chest, like I couldn’t pick which thing to tackle first, so I just sat there scrolling my phone for ten minutes. I still get everything done eventually, but it feels like I’m barely treading water instead of swimming.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I do feel a little down some evenings, but I still drift off once my head hits the pillow. There’ve been maybe two nights this week when I laid there for twenty minutes running through the next day’s to-do list, but I wouldn’t call it real trouble—more like a brief delay. Once I’m asleep I stay out until she wakes me for her feed.
I have felt sad or miserable

I get waves of it—like yesterday afternoon the house felt really quiet, she was napping, and I just sat on the couch with this heavy, gloomy feeling for maybe half an hour. It lifts when someone texts or I keep busy, but at least once a day I’ll feel that little cloud settle for a bit.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A couple of times this week—nothing dramatic, just tears sliding down while I’m washing bottles. Once was after her check-up: everything went great, but once I got home I sat in the car and cried for maybe two minutes. It’s like the relief valve pops and then I’m okay again.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I get tired and teary, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I just want to feel more like myself again.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary

Patient-reported symptoms
- Anhedonia: diminished pleasure in previously enjoyable activities; laughter feels “thin,” food “muted.”
- Low mood: daily waves of sadness or “heavy, gloomy” feelings; brief crying spells 2×/week unrelated to external stressors.
- Excessive guilt/self-blame: attributes infant fussing to personal failure; ruminates over perceived parenting mistakes.
- Anxiety: recurrent, sudden “what-if” worries (feeding safety, break-in) with brief heart racing; no full panic attacks.
- Overwhelm: chest pressure and task paralysis when multiple demands coincide; describes “treading water.”
- Sleep: generally falls asleep easily; occasional 20-min delay while planning next day.
- Self-harm: denies any thoughts of harming self.

Pattern
Mild-to-moderate mood and anxiety symptoms present daily but fluctuating; no safety concerns identified.

Screening significance
Meets several criteria warranting further evaluation for postpartum depression and/or anxiety (anhedonia, low mood, tearfulness, guilt, anxiety surges, impaired coping).

Risk factors noted
- Persistent sadness with loss of enjoyment
- Self-blame/guilt out of proportion to events
- Recurrent intrusive worries and physiological anxiety
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed

Recommendation (screening only)
Refer for comprehensive assessment with obstetric or mental health provider to determine diagnosis and appropriate level of care.
